title: Starter rituals for engineers — pricing & quickstart voice
body:
Purpose:
This doc is a lightweight playbook of positioning lines, short quickstarts and pricing-language specifically aimed at engineers evaluating the Hosted API for their first integration. Goal: reduce perceived onboarding cost and time-to-first-success, while being explicit about unit economics so teams can make a quick go/no-go decision.

Audience & evaluation moments:
- Individual engineer building a prototype (fast time-to-result, low friction)
- Small team validating model fit (repeatable perf, predictable cost)
- Platform/infra engineer assessing long-term operating model (routing, SLA, dedicated capacity tradeoffs)

Key one-line value props (engineer-centric):
1) "Run a useful model in minutes — curl to working output, no infra dance."
2) "Consistent latency you can measure — realistic defaults, predictable costs."
3) "Same API if you later pin capacity or move to private infra — migrate, don’t rewrite."

Three starter rituals (quickstarts optimized for conversion)
A. Hello-result (0–5 minutes) — curl-first ritual
- Prompt: single-sentence example that returns a trimmed, useful answer (e.g., `curl -X POST /v1/infer -d '{"prompt":"Summarize: <text>"}'`)
- Win criteria: developer gets a meaningful output in < 30s and sees token usage in the response
- Microcopy for docs: "Try this now — it runs in seconds and shows exact cost for the call."

B. SDK + test harness (5–15 minutes) — verification ritual
- Ship an SDK sample (node/python) that includes: example prompt templates, retry policy, and a local unit test that asserts response shape and a token budget assertion
- Win criteria: test passes locally, dev copies sample into repo, sees cost per test in comments
- Microcopy for README: "Clone, npm install, run `npm test`. You’ll see the exact request, response and cost in the test output."

C. Real-ish load (15–60 minutes) — smoke & economics ritual
- Provide a tiny harness (docker-compose) that sends a representative traffic pattern, measures p50/p95 latency and aggregated token spend over 1 minute
- Win criteria: team can estimate monthly bill for projected usage with a provided calculator
- Docs snippet: "Run `./smoke.sh` and paste numbers into our cost calculator to see your estimated monthly spend."

Pricing-language drafts (simple, engineer-friendly frames)
- Keep ngrams short and operational: avoid abstract terms. Focus on units (tokens, embeddings) + examples.
- 3 framing lines to test in microcopy:
  • "Pay only for what you call: per-token billing with exact token counts returned in the response."
  • "Free starter credits and sample traffic so your prototype has a real budget to run."
  • "Committed pools if you need predictable throughput — convert any hosted usage into Reserved capacity."

Concrete microcopy examples (for docs, signup, modal)
- Signup banner: "Start building: $50 starter credits, no card for 14 days. Try a working example in under 5 minutes."
- Cost tooltip (API response UI): "This call used 72 tokens (~$0.002). See how batching or caching can cut that in half."
- Pricing FAQ blurb: "Tokens are counted on input + output. Embeddings billed per vector; reranking calls bill for both the scoring prompt and the candidate inputs."

Competitive calls-to-action (how we nudge engineers away from rolling their own)
- Emphasize operational friction and hidden cost of DIY: "You can run models locally today, but we make serving them at scale predictable — autoscaling policies, KV cache, and kernel-level optimizations are already configured."
- Differentiator line: "Same API surface between hosted and private deployments — switch to Dedicated without changing your code."

Pricing pitfalls to avoid in messaging
- Don’t bury per-token math in long prose — show an example call with tokens and converted cost inline.
- Avoid calling out complex tiers on the first screen. Offer a link: "How pricing works (short explainer)."
- Be explicit about burst behaviour: "Short bursts are supported; sustained throughput may need a reserved pool."

Suggested A/B tests (early experiments)
1) CTA copy on quickstart doc: "Try a live example in 60s" vs "Run this curl and see the exact cost" — measure signup-to-first-success conversion
2) Pricing microcopy: show example cost inline vs hide cost behind a hover — measure trust (time-on-page) and conversion
3) Starter credits phrasing: "$50 credits, no card" vs "Free credits when you sign up" — measure friction and abuse rates

Measurement & success metrics
- Primary: % of new signups that run a successful quickstart call within 24 hours
- Secondary: % of quickstart users who convert to an active project (5k tokens/month) within 30 days
- Product signal: average token cost per successful quickstart call; time to first meaningful response

Open questions for product/engineering
- Can the response include the exact token count and estimated cost by default for quickstart keys?
- Do we want an opt-in tiny smoke harness in our SDK that sends a single representative profiling call and returns p50/p95?
- How to surface default caching/batching recommendations in the quickstart without requiring a console visit?

Next steps (short runway)
- Build 3-minute curl example and ensure response includes token count (owner: docs, ETA: 1 week)
- Wire a small A/B experiment in the quickstart docs (owner: growth, ETA: 2 weeks)
- Draft modal microcopy and pricing tooltip for review with legal (owner: GTM, ETA: 1 week)

Appendix: example copy snippets to copy/paste
- Quickstart headline: "From curl to result in under 60 seconds — see request, response, and cost."
- README install line: "pip install redwood-sdk — run `python hello.py` to get a live output and the cost for the call."
- Pricing line for landing page: "Simple per-token billing, clear usage dashboard, and credits to get you started."

Notes on tone: be pragmatic, engineer-respecting (show data), avoid marketing hyperbole. Let the quickstart do the convincing — short, verifiable wins beat long claim lists.
